readings.title: Large-scale cluster management at Google with Borg

read_scope.text: Complete main prose sections 1 through 8.3, physical pages 1–14.
read_scope.visual: Figures 5 (p7) and 12 (p10) rendered and inspected; other captions and surrounding prose read.

evidence.claim: Admission can leave tasks pending; production band forbids self-preemption.
Placement combines failure spread, package locality, preemption cost and multidimensional packing; spreading fragments capacity and tight packing exposes underestimated requests.
Preemption kills/requeues; application recovery uses durable state/checkpoints, with no assured notice.
Static snapshot compaction studies packing, not completion replay; some constraints are relaxed and a small fraction of picky tasks may remain pending.
Runtime interference remains; compressible resources can throttle while reclaimed noncompressible memory can kill batch tasks. Greedy latency-sensitive CPU is capped to avoid long batch starvation.

card.trigger: Place mixed latency-sensitive services and interruptible long-running batch work on shared machines.
card.problem: Reconcile packing, bursts, correlated failures and batch progress; occupancy is not useful completion.
card.mechanism: Evaluate placement dimensions with runtime resource controls; name preempted-work recovery owner and admission boundary.
card.limits: Static packing evidence does not establish completion or ongoing-service latency; not every shared-resource effect is eliminated.
card.counterexample: Repeatedly evicted long batch work consumes CPU without durable progress; dedicated placement can be justified despite packing cost.
card.verification: Compare shared/separated and spread/tight placement; measure pending age/reasons, service latency, durable batch progress, lost/repeated CPU work, memory kills and runnable delay; exercise kill without notice and repeated reclaim.

provider_results.limits: Snapshot compaction is not completion evidence; historical chroot/cgroups are not adopted as an untrusted-code security recommendation.

readings.title: Omega: flexible, scalable schedulers for large compute clusters

read_scope.text: All 14 pages extracted locally: sections 1–8, acknowledgments, reference metadata, all figure captions and surrounding prose.

readings.retrieval_gap: Web PDF fetch rejected application/octet-stream; bounded local HTTPS fetch and pypdf extraction succeeded.

evidence.claim: Slow placement causes planner head-of-line blocking; fixed pools fragment resources and exclusive offers can lock capacity during decisions.
Parallel planners use refreshed local cell-state copies and validated atomic commits; conflicting claims retry. Incremental task placement differs from all-or-nothing gang transactions.
Common allocation/precedence rules are enforced; strict global fairness and starvation guarantees remain separate/future work.
Coarse conflict detection and universal gang semantics cause additional retries; gang use depends on actual job needs.
Opportunistic MapReduce acceleration uses an idealized linear performance model and incomplete worker setup accounting.

card.trigger: Expensive service placement blocks simpler jobs or different job classes need independent placement policies.
card.problem: Serialize all planning or partition resources and lose flexibility/packing.
card.mechanism: Plan concurrently over full shared state; validate resource claims, resynchronize on conflict, and choose incremental or gang transaction semantics per job.
card.limits: Redoing conflicted planning costs time; physical execution capacity and fairness/starvation require separate policies.
card.counterexample: A slow planner repeatedly loses a contested resource to fast planners; no bounded start time follows from parallel planning.
card.verification: Race two claims for one slot; require one owner, refresh before retry, no over-allocation; test partial/gang utility, planning delay, conflicts, actual start, durable completion and starvation.

provider_results.kind: Google trace-driven and synthetic simulations plus simplified acceleration model
provider_results.limits: Do not transfer historical Mesos/YARN comparisons to current versions; do not use potential acceleration as a measured result or acceptance threshold.

readings.title: Building resilient multi-tenant systems with Amazon SQS fair queues

read_scope.text: Complete main article Overview through Conclusion, Java producer snippet, metrics and example-application explanation, six figure captions.

evidence.claim: Prioritizes quiet-tenant delivery using in-flight distribution; long processing and high volume can both produce imbalance.
MessageGroupId on standard queues identifies tenants without imposing per-group FIFO order or per-tenant consumption-rate limits.
Quiet-group queue metrics distinguish tenant impact from whole-queue backlog; figures/sample are provider illustration, not our experiment.

card.trigger: Noisy or slow tenants in a shared standard queue inflate quiet tenants’ waiting.
card.problem: Global queue age hides tenant outcomes and message counts underprice expensive work.
card.mechanism: Meaningful MessageGroupId and quiet-prioritized delivery plus tenant-specific dwell/cost observations.
card.limits: Delivery fairness is not per-tenant rate enforcement, strict ordering, worker reservation or preemption; current detection differs from launch explanation.
card.counterexample: Every worker already runs a nonpreemptible long job; changing the next delivery cannot free a slot. Fabricated tenant identities invalidate intended grouping.
card.verification: Fast/slow/high-volume labeled and unlabeled inputs; measure queue dwell, prefetch residency, processing cost, useful completions, redelivery and eventual noisy-tenant progress.

provider_results.kind: Provider explanation, sample application and dashboard illustration
provider_results.limits: No quantitative hard latency or worker scheduling guarantee adopted.

assumptions: Deadlines label usefulness; do not cancel expired work
A3/A4 wait in durable backlog outside worker ownership
Cap includes prefetched, retrying, blocked and executing A ownership
No A borrowing of quiet reserve

protected.policy: Hard A resident/in-flight cap 2, including prefetch; remaining 2 slots reserved for B/C; no borrowing.

independent_review.method: Independent in-memory arithmetic from supplied inputs/intervals; no writes.
confirmed: Common horizon avoids misleading utilization comparison
counterexamples: Hidden prefetch holds spare slots unless counted
A deadline 10 reverses success of A3/A4
More than two simultaneous quiet arrivals invalidate all-quiet deadline claim
Dropping FIFO expired B/C reduces cost to 32 slot-seconds

local_execution.method: Python interval sweep against fixed expected arithmetic; resource capacity, A cap, arrivals/durations, costs and quiet waiting/useful counts checked.
local_execution.scope: Finite arithmetic only; no scheduler implementation or runtime/broker experiment.

concurrent_claim.input: Two independent planners observe one free resource slot; fast claim commits first, slow claim conflicts and refreshes.
concurrent_claim.expected: One owner maximum. Second placement cannot commit until resource release and fresh validation.
concurrent_claim.limit: Does not prove bounded retry or starvation; explicit policy required.

multidimensional_fit.input: Two nodes, each free 4 CPUs/8 GiB; single-node job requires 2 CPUs/10 GiB.
multidimensional_fit.limit: Aggregate memory does not fit a single-node execution; splitting requires an actual distributed job model.

security_boundary: Placement spread, fair groups and resource throttles are not application data authorization, credential, network or untrusted-code isolation boundaries.
